title: private-deploy networking incident breadcrumbs - VPC peering / DNS / TLS / egress
content:
Quick breadcrumbs for the private deployment networking incident affecting customer 'acme-x' (reported 2026-03-02).

Summary / symptom:
- Customer's app in their VPC cannot reach Redwood private control plane endpoints (control-plane.example.redwood.net) from their private subnets when deployed behind our peering connection.
- From their bastion: curl -v https://control-plane.example.redwood.net -> TLS handshake times out / or connection resets depending on host. DNS sometimes resolves, sometimes NXDOMAIN depending on which instance/az.
- Intermittent egress: some pods/instances can reach external internet, others cannot. Suspect route table or NAT gateway + VPC peering config + DNS over peering.

Commands / outputs tried (raw, chronological):

1) DNS checks from customer bastion (us-east-1b):
$ dig +short control-plane.example.redwood.net @10.0.0.2
10.10.5.23

$ dig +trace control-plane.example.redwood.net
; <<>> DiG 9.16.1-Ubuntu <<>> +trace control-plane.example.redwood.net
;; ->>HEADER<<- opcode: QUERY, status: NOERROR, id: 12345
;; Received 512 bytes
.           518400 IN NS a.root-servers.net.
...
;; Received 112 bytes
control-plane.example.redwood.net. 300 IN A 10.10.5.23

Notes: direct query to the resolver on 10.0.0.2 sometimes returns NXDOMAIN (seen from other AZ). Suspect split-horizon / route to resolver inconsistent across subnets.

2) VPC peering checks via AWS CLI (my account access)
$ aws ec2 describe-vpc-peering-connections --filters Name=requester-vpc-info.vpc-id,Values=vpc-0abcd1234
{
  "VpcPeeringConnections": [
    {
      "VpcPeeringConnectionId": "pcx-07f12abc",
      "Status": {"Code": "active","Message": "Active"},
      "AccepterVpcInfo": {"VpcId": "vpc-0f12ab34", "CidrBlock": "10.10.0.0/16"},
      "RequesterVpcInfo": {"VpcId": "vpc-0abcd1234", "CidrBlock": "10.0.0.0/16"}
    }
  ]
}

- Peering is Active. BUT: vpc-peering does not support transitive routing. Need explicit route entries on both sides.

3) Route tables (customer side) - important route missing observed:
$ aws ec2 describe-route-tables --filters Name=vpc-id,Values=vpc-0abcd1234
--- route table excerpts ---
Destination: 10.10.0.0/16 -> pcx-07f12abc
Destination: 0.0.0.0/0 -> igw-0a1b2c3d

Customer has some private subnets that route 0.0.0.0/0 to a NAT instance in a different AZ which is temporarily unhealthy.

4) tcpdump on bastion when curl times out:
$ sudo tcpdump -n host 10.10.5.23 and port 443 -w trace.pcap
Observations:
- SYN sent from bastion (public IP) -> SYN/ACK not returned when routed via peer sometimes.
- When connection resets: see RST from 10.10.5.23 occasionally.

5) traceroute from affected instance to control-plane:
$ traceroute -n 10.10.5.23
 1  10.0.1.1  0.7 ms  0.6 ms  0.5 ms
 2  10.0.254.1  1.4 ms  1.2 ms  1.3 ms
 3  10.10.5.23  7.8 ms  8.0 ms  7.9 ms
Looks normal on route plane.

6) TLS handshake debug (openssl):
$ openssl s_client -connect control-plane.example.redwood.net:443 -servername control-plane.example.redwood.net -msg -brief
CONNECTED(00000003)
write to 0x7f9c0e3b:errno=104
139768645298688:error:140770FC:SSL routines:SSL23_GET_SERVER_HELLO:unknown protocol:s23_clnt.c:802:

Sometimes works from same host after retry -> suggests middlebox or inconsistent egress path.

7) Check security groups / NACLs
- Security groups allow outbound 443 from customer subnets to 10.10.5.0/24.
- NACLs are wide-open (allow ephemeral ranges). No obvious block.

8) K8s/kube-proxy logs on customer side (for pods failing to egress):
- iptables SNAT chains show missing MASQUERADE on one node due to kube-proxy crash-restart earlier today. Pods on that node had no SNAT -> responses don't go back out correctly.
- Fixed by restarting kube-proxy, but issue persisted for other hosts.

9) AWS NAT gateway status
- In one AZ NAT gw associated was showing 'impaired' (cloudwatch metrics show very high error rates). Customer had fallback NAT instance but iptables there misconfigured.

Hypotheses (short):
- Primary: Route table + NAT health + kube-proxy SNAT issues causing asymmetric routing; some flows go via peering/VPC but replies egress via IGW/NAT -> gets dropped.
- Secondary: DNS resolution inconsistent because cross-account VPC peering needs enableDnsResolutionFromRemoteVpc / enableDnsHostnames. One side didn't have 'enableDnsSupport' or the resolver IP is not reachable from some subnets.
- Tertiary: TLS handshake failures due to SNI/TCP middlebox (corporate proxy) intercepting TLS — but likely symptom of broken TCP path rather than real MITM.

Immediate fixes applied:
- Restarted kube-proxy on 2 affected nodes -> restored SNAT for pods on those nodes.
- Replaced impaired NAT gateway with a new NAT gateway in same AZ and associated Elastic IP.
- Updated route table to ensure 10.10.0.0/16 -> pcx-07f12abc present on all private route tables (confirmed via aws cli). NOTE: need to push same on acceptance side too (we asked infra team to confirm our side routes).
- Asked infra to enable VPC peering attribute: enable-dns-support and enable-dns-hostnames checked on both VPCs.

Remaining / flapping behaviors observed:
- DNS sometimes still resolves differently depending on instance resolver. Likely due to local caching (systemd-resolved) and inconsistent route to resolver during peering failover.
- A few TLS handshake failures remain for one customer node — I suspect intermittent packet drops (seen in tcpdump) causing handshake to fail. Need deeper packet capture for full handshake.

Next steps / TODOs:
- [ ] Get infra to confirm routes on Redwood side: ensure route tables pointing back to requester CIDR via pcx-07f12abc (both sides).
- [ ] Validate VPC peering DNS attributes enabled (both sides) and document whether Private Hosted Zone association would be better (Route53 private hosted zone shared vs peering behavior).
- [ ] Collect full tcpdump on affected node during controlled retry (port 443) and share pcap with neteng / infra for packet-level analysis.
- [ ] Ask customer to temporarily disable any corporate outbound proxies to rule out TLS interception.
- [ ] Add synthetic checks from each AZ to control-plane.example.redwood.net to detect which AZs are failing and correlate with NAT gateway metrics.
- [ ] Create runbook steps for future: verify NAT health, kube-proxy SNAT, peering route table parity, resolver reachability.

Notes / ochre:
- Important to remember: VPC peering DNS resolution only works when enableDnsSupport and enableDnsHostnames are set and if using the remote VPC's resolver IP (usually .2). If customer has custom resolvers or forwarding rules, behavior will vary.
- VPC peering won't transfer IGW/NAT gw traffic for transitive routes; must ensure replies' path matches request path or use Transit Gateway.

Attachments / artifacts I've saved:
- pcap: /tmp/acmex-2026-03-04-controlplane-trace.pcap
- aws cli output dumps: /tmp/acmex-route-tables.json
- quick notes posted to ENG-1423 (see linked_artifacts)

If needed, ping me (mira) or oliver for live debugging window tomorrow 08:00-11:00 PT. Will try to reproduce with controlled curl + tcpdump and get full handshake capture.

-- mira
